Triftosylhydrazones

and Xihe Bi*

ABSTRACT: Here, we report a general and practical Doyle−
Kirmse reaction of allyl/propargyl sulfides with donor-only vinyl
carbenes generated in situ from vinyl triftosylhydrazones in the
presence of a silver catalyst. This protocol features mild conditions,
exhibits a broad substrate scope and exceptional functional group
tolerance, and provides corresponding 1,5-dienyl and 1,4-enallenyl
sulfides in high yields. Moreover, gram-scale synthesis, late-stage modifications of complex molecules, and post-synthetic
transformations were performed to demonstrate the applicability of this protocol.
[2,3]-Sigmatropic rearrangements of onium ylides are an
important and fundamental transformation in organic chem-
istry for synthesizing valuable heteroatom-containing com-
pounds with high stereoselectivity.
1
Among these, the [2,3]-
sigmatropic rearrangement of sulfonium ylides generated from
carbenes and allyl/propargyl sulfides, known as the Doyle−
Kirmse (D−K) reaction,
2
offers a potentially general method
for the stereoselective construction of a high-value sulfur-
containing quaternary or tertiary carbon center, which has
found applications in the synthesis of bioactive molecules and
natural products. Over the decades, various transition metal
and metal-free D−K reactions using tetramethylsilane (TMS)-
stabilized
3
or electron-withdrawing group (EWG)-derived
diazo reagents
4−7
as well as a few donor-only diazomethane
reagents
8
and N-sulfonyl-1,2,3-triazoles
9
as carbene precursors
have been established. In contrast, the utilization of α-vinyl
diazo compounds in D−K reactions remains challenging and
scarcely explored because of their propensity to undergo
intramolecular cyclization to form pyrazoles.
10
Despite these
challenges, Wang and Feng’s groups successfully employed
vinyl diazoacetates
4e
or vinyldiazo compounds with chiral
Oppolzer’s camphor sultam
6a
or pyrazoleamide
6b
auxiliary as
vinylcarbene precursors for the enantioselective D−K reaction
(Figure 1A). However, to the best of our knowledge, there has
been no general catalytic system for the D−K reaction with
donor-substituted α-vinyldiazomethanes as carbene precursors
to date due to their inherent reactivity. A single example of a
rhodium-catalyzed D−K reaction of phenyl allyl sulfide with in
situ generated vinyldiazomethane from tosylhydrazone was
found in a report by Wang and co-workers, although providing
the desired product in 48% yield.
8a
In 2015, Wang and co-
workers used cyclopropenes as vinylcarbene precursors in the
D−K reaction to bypass the general reactivity issues of α-
vinyldiazomethanes as donor diazo compounds (Figure 1A).
11
Recently, we discovered vinyl triftosylhydrazones as easily
decomposable diazo surrogates and addressed the general issue
of the reactivity of α-vinyldiazomethane toward pyrazole
formation by merging it with a bulky silver catalyst to generate
highly electrophilic silver vinylcarbenes.
12
Encouraged by our
success in transition-metal-catalyzed carbene transfer reactions
using vinyl triftosylhydrazones as vinylcarbene precursors,
13,14
we envision that the merger of vinyl triftosylhydrazones with
silver catalysis might govern the highly efficient D−K reaction

efficient silver-catalyzed D−K reaction between allyl/propargyl
sulfides and α-vinyldiazomethanes derived from vinyl trifto-
sylhydrazones (Figure 1B). This approach provides practical
access to diverse 1,5-dienyl or 1,4-enallenyl sulfides with high
efficiency. Dienyl sulfides are valuable core structures in
biologically active molecules and versatile building blocks for
the synthesis of value-added products.
15

cinnamyl N-sulfonyl hydrazone 1 and allyl phenyl sulfide 2,

Interestingly,
when an excessive amount of triftosylhydrazone 1a was
employed, product 3 preferentially underwent cyclopropyla-

With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we explored
the scope of vinyl triftosylhydrazones derived from various α,β-
unsaturated aldehydes, using allyl phenyl sulfide 2 as the
reaction partner (Scheme 1). A variety of α-(arylvinyl)
triftosylhydrazones, bearing electron-withdrawing or electron-
donating substituents at the para, meta, or ortho position of the
aryl ring, were well-tolerated and provided the desired 1,5-
dienyl sulfides 3−20 in high to excellent yields. Vinyl
triftosylhydrazones containing medicinally relevant (hetero)-
aryl rings, such as naphthalene, furan, and thiophene,
underwent the reaction smoothly, affording the target products
21−23 in good yields. This silver-catalyzed system was also
applicable to vinyl triftosylhydrazones bearing non-aryl
substituents, including methyl (24 and 29), n-butyl (25),
phenylethyl (26), cyclohexyl (27), and (phenylmethoxy)-
methyl (28) groups. Likewise, a set of 3,3-disubstituted and
2,3-disubstituted vinyl triftosylhydrazones could also be
effectively activated by the current conditions, leading to the
formation of multisubstituted 1,5-dienyl sulfide products 30−
34 in 48−84% yields. 2,4-Pentadienal-derived triftosylhydra-
zones also serve as suitable substrates, furnishing correspond-
ing 1,5,7-trienyl sulfide products 35 and 36 in 74 and 55%,
respectively, which are common skeletons in bioactive natural
products and drug molecules.
19
Finally, we examined the
reactivity of vinyl triftosylhydrazones derived from α,β-
unsaturated ketones, which underwent smooth reaction to
deliver desired 1,5-dienyl sulfides containing a quaternary
carbon center in good yields (37−39). These compounds
represent the most potent inhibitors of stromelysin-1.
20
Next, we surveyed the scope of allyl sulfides using vinyl
triftosylhydrazone 1a as the constant coupling reagent
(Scheme 2A). Aryl allyl sulfides substituted with various
substituents, such as methyl, methoxy, isopropyl, halogens, and
trifluoromethyl groups, reacted smoothly to afford correspond-

ing products 40−51 in good to excellent yields. Replacing the
phenyl ring of aryl allyl sulfides with electron-rich naphthalene
(52) and thiophene (53) rings afforded the desired product in
high yields, while 2-methyl furyl allyl sulfide (54) resulted in a
poor yield. Similarly, benzyl-, alkyl-, alkyl ester-, and allyl-
substituted allyl sulfides (55−59) were also compatible with
the reaction conditions. In the case of diallyl sulfide, the
desired product 59 was exclusively obtained in 80% yield
under standard conditions. Intriguingly, upon adjustment of
the stoichiometric ratio of compound 1a to diallyl sulfide from
1:2 to 2:1, no detectable double D−K reaction product was
observed. Instead, product 59 was isolated in 63% yield, along
with side products resulting from cyclopropanation and self-
cyclization (Scheme S2 of the Supporting Information). The
reaction demonstrated a high tolerance of various function-
alities, such as methyl (60), phenyl (61), halogens (62 and
63), and azide (64), on the vinyl unit of aryl allyl sulfides,
furnishing target products in 51−85% yields. Sterically
hindered 1,1-dimethylallyl aryl sulfide could still provide the
desired product 65 in a high yield. Likewise, the current
protocol was suitable for cyclohex-2-enyl aryl sulfide, giving
desired product 66 in 49% yield with moderate diastereose-
lectivity (49% yield, dr = 7:2). Finally, the scope of this
reaction was successfully extended to propargyl sulfides,
thereby providing a convenient route to synthetically useful
1,4-enallenyl sulfides (Scheme 2B).
21
However, a slight
modification from the original conditions, such as changing
the base from NaH to CsF, is necessary to achieve a
synthetically useful yield (see Tables S6−S9 of the Supporting
Information). Under these modified conditions, aryl propargyl
sulfides with methyl, isopropyl, tert-butyl, and chloro
functionality at the para position of the aryl ring reacted
smoothly to afford corresponding 1,4-enallenyl sulfides 67−71
in 50−58% yields.
To further demonstrate the practicality of this protocol, we
performed a 5 mmol scale reaction between vinyl triftosylhy-
drazone 1a and allyl phenyl sulfide 2, resulting in the successful
formation of product 3 in 92% (1.23 g) isolated yield (Scheme
3A). The synthetic value of formed products 3 and 64 was
then demonstrated. Oxidation of compound 3 with m-
chloroperbenzoic acid (m-CPBA) produced sulfone 72 in
90% yield. Pleasingly, compound 64 could undergo Cu(I)-
catalyzed azide−alkyne cycloaddition to obtain medicinally
significant triazole 74 in 95% yield.
22
The late-stage
modification of complex molecules, such as perillaldehyde
and fluvastatin-decorated vinyl triftosylhydrazones, was also
possible, giving products 75 and 76 in 54 and 71% yields,

Finally, a series of control experiments were conducted to
elucidate the reaction mechanism (Scheme 3C). First, the
reaction of vinyl triftosylhydrazone 1a with benzyl phenyl
sulfide 77 failed to yield the Stevens rearrangement product 78
under standard conditions, which could rule out a probable
[1,2]-sigmatropic rearrangement. Next, we performed reac-
tions between vinyl triftosylhydrazone 1a and cinnamyl tolyl
sulfide 79 with different Ag(I) catalysts. The diastereoselec-
tivity (dr) of product 80 was consistently determined to be 2:1,
regardless of the silver catalyst or its associated ligands. Based
on the above observations and previous literature, this sivler-
catalyzed [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement likely proceeds via a
metal-free ylide intermediate (Scheme S4 of the Supporting
Information).

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that the merger of
vinyl triftosylhydrazones with silver catalysis enabled the highly
efficient D−K reaction of sulfides with donor-substituted
vinyldiazomethanes. The bulky and weakly coordinated
Tp
(CF
3
)
2
Ag catalyst is capable of activating donor-only α-
vinyldiazomethanes under mild conditions toward the D−K
reaction of diverse allyl/propargyl sulfides, affording medici-
nally interesting 1,5-dienyl and 1,4-enallenyl sulfides with high
catalytic efficiency. The asymmetric D−K reaction of allyl
sulfides with vinyl triftosylhydrazones is under exploration and
will be reported in due course (for preliminary experimental
results, see Scheme S1 of the Supporting Information).

[2,3]-Sigmatropic rearrangements of onium ylides are an
important and fundamental transformation in organic chem-
istry for synthesizing valuable heteroatom-containing com-
pounds with high stereoselectivity.<sup>1</sup> Among these, the [2,3]-
sigmatropic rearrangement of sulfonium ylides generated from
carbenes and allyl/propargyl sulfides, known as the Doyle−
Kirmse (D−K) reaction,<sup>2</sup> ofers a potentially general method
for the stereoselective construction of a high-value sulfur-
containing quaternary or tertiary carbon center, which has
found applications in the synthesis of bioactive molecules and
natural products. Over the decades, various transition metal
and metal-free D−K reactions using tetramethylsilane (TMS)-
stabilized<sup>3</sup> or electron-withdrawing group (EWG)-derived
diazo reagents<sup>4−7</sup> as well as a few donor-only diazomethane
reagents<sup>8</sup> and N-sulfonyl-1,2,3-triazoles<sup>9</sup> as carbene precursors
have been established. In contrast, the utilization of α-vinyl
diazo compounds in D−K reactions remains challenging and
scarcely explored because of their propensity to undergo
intramolecular cyclization to form pyrazoles.<sup>10</sup> Despite these
challenges, Wang and Feng’s groups successfully employed
vinyl diazoacetates<sup>4e</sup> or vinyldiazo compounds with chiral
Oppolzer’s camphor sultam<sup>6a</sup> or pyrazoleamide<sup>6b</sup> auxiliary as
vinylcarbene precursors for the enantioselective D−K reaction
(Figure 1A). However, to the best of our knowledge, there has
been no general catalytic system for the D−K reaction with
donor-substituted α-vinyldiazomethanes as carbene precursors
to date due to their inherent reactivity. A single example of a
rhodium-catalyzed D−K reaction of phenyl allyl sulfide with in
situ generated vinyldiazomethane from tosylhydrazone was
found in a report by Wang and co-workers, although providing
the desired product in 48% yield.<sup>8a</sup> In 2015, Wang and co-
workers used cyclopropenes as vinylcarbene precursors in the
D−K reaction to bypass the general reactivity issues of α-
vinyldiazomethanes as donor diazo compounds (Figure 1A).<sup>11</sup>
Figure 1. Background and motivation of the present work.

success in transition-metal-catalyzed carbene transfer reactions
using vinyl triftosylhydrazones as vinylcarbene precursors,<sup>13,14</sup>
we envision that the merger of vinyl triftosylhydrazones with
silver catalysis might govern the highly eficient D−K reaction
